warmup.q: A month-end statement job runs on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Each merchant's task submits a ledger query to the same pool and calls get() on it. With 5 merchants it takes 2 seconds. With 400 merchants, what happens?
options: It takes about 80 times longer, because the pool is busy
The pool grows past 20 threads to keep up
It hangs forever with the CPU near zero
The JVM detects the deadlock and throws in one of the tasks
warmup.why: The first 20 merchant tasks take every thread, and each one waits for a query that is queued behind 380 other merchant tasks. No thread will ever be free to run a query, so the job hangs. A fixed pool never grows, and the JVM's deadlock detector looks for cycles of locks, not tasks waiting on queued tasks, so nothing throws.

sections.h: Name your threads, and know where failures go
sections.html:
The default names are pool-3-thread-7. In a thread dump of a service with eight pools, that tells you nothing. Name them, and the name shows up in every log line that prints the thread, in every thread dump and in every profiler:

Java
ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory();   // JDK 21+: ledger-0, ledger-1, ...
ExecutorService ledgerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, named);
Kotlin
val named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory()            // JDK 21+: ledger-0, ledger-1, ...
val ledgerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, named)

Before JDK 21 you write a small ThreadFactory with an AtomicInteger, or use Guava's ThreadFactoryBuilder.

Now failures. Lesson 1 of this track showed that execute and submit treat an exception differently, and in production the difference decides whether you ever hear about it.

With execute, the exception escapes the task. The worker thread dies, its UncaughtExceptionHandler runs, and the pool starts a new thread in its place. The default handler prints a stack trace to System.err, outside your logging framework and its request ids.

With submit, the FutureTask catches the exception and keeps it. Nothing is printed. If nobody calls get(), which is normal for fire-and-forget work, the failure is gone.

So an UncaughtExceptionHandler on the thread factory covers only half the cases. To cover both, catch failures in one place that every task passes through. submit, invokeAll and CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, pool) all end up in execute, so a ThreadPoolExecutor subclass that overrides execute and wraps each task sees everything. Report the failure there, with the request id, and don't rethrow: rethrowing only kills the worker and prints the same stack trace a second time. The lab builds exactly that pool.

try.title: Find out who hears about a failure
steps: Run FailureDemo. Its threads are named ledger-N and have an UncaughtExceptionHandler.
Before you run it, predict for each case: does the handler print, and which thread runs the next task?

code.title: FailureDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory; /** Named threads with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Which failures does the handler see? */ public class FailureDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("ledger-", 0) // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... .uncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) -> System.out.println(" handler: " + t.getName() + " died of " + e)) .factory(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, factory)) { System.out.println("1. execute() a task that throws"); pool.execute(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("ledger row locked"); }); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println(" the next task runs on " + pool.submit(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).get()); System.out.println("2. submit() a task that throws"); Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("negative amount"); }); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println(" (nothing printed) the next task runs on " + pool.submit(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).get()); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println(" only get() shows it: " + e.getCause()); } } } }

alt.title: FailureDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Named threads with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Which failures does the handler see? */ fun main() { val factory = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("ledger-", 0) // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... .uncaughtExceptionHandler { t, e -> println(" handler: ${t.name} died of $e") } .factory() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, factory).use { pool -> println("1. execute() a task that throws") pool.execute { throw IllegalStateException("ledger row locked") } Thread.sleep(200) println(" the next task runs on " + pool.submit<String> { Thread.currentThread().name }.get()) println("2. submit() a task that throws") val f = pool.submit<Unit> { throw IllegalStateException("negative amount") } Thread.sleep(200) println(" (nothing printed) the next task runs on " + pool.submit<String> { Thread.currentThread().name }.get()) try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println(" only get() shows it: ${e.cause}") } } }

try.expect: For execute, the handler prints ledger-0 died of ... ledger row locked, and the next task runs on ledger-1: the pool replaced the dead worker. For submit, nothing prints, the next task still runs on ledger-1, and the exception only appears when get() is called.

sections.h: Carry the request context across the hand-off
sections.html:
SLF4J's MDC, the current tracing span and the authenticated principal usually live in ThreadLocals. When you hand a task to a pool, they don't come along. The worker's ThreadLocal is empty, or it still holds a value that an earlier task left behind. Then the ledger write you are trying to trace during an incident logs no request id at all, or the wrong one.

The fix has three steps: capture the value on the submitting thread, install it on the worker before the task runs, and put the worker's old value back afterwards:

Java
static Runnable withRequestId(Runnable task) {
    String captured = RequestContext.get();            // 1. on the submitting thread
    return () -> {
        String previous = RequestContext.get();
        RequestContext.set(captured);                  // 2. on the worker
        try {
            task.run();
        } finally {
            if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear(); else RequestContext.set(previous);   // 3. never leak
        }
    };
}
Kotlin
fun withRequestId(task: Runnable): Runnable {
    val captured = RequestContext.get()                // 1. on the submitting thread
    return Runnable {
        val previous = RequestContext.get()
        RequestContext.set(captured)                   // 2. on the worker
        try {
            task.run()
        } finally {
            if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear() else RequestContext.set(previous)   // 3. never leak
        }
    }
}

The capture must happen in the method that is called on the submitting thread. Read the ThreadLocal inside the lambda and you read the worker's value, which is the bug you set out to fix. The finally matters as much: pool threads are reused, so whatever a task leaves behind is the next task's context.

Don't make every caller remember to wrap. Wrap once, in the executor that everyone uses, as the lab does. MicroProfile Context Propagation's ManagedExecutor, which Quarkus provides, does the same for the contexts it knows about.

Virtual threads don't change any of this: a new thread starts with empty ThreadLocals, except inheritable ones. Scoped values, final in JDK 25, are the newer tool for request context, and the virtual threads track covers them.

try.title: Lose a request id, then leak one
steps: Run ContextDemo. The main thread sets req-42 and submits three tasks to a pool with one thread.
Predict all three lines before you look. For line 3, find the task that caused it.

code.title: ContextDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** A request id in a ThreadLocal, handed to a pool three ways. */ public class ContextDemo { static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>(); // capture on the submitting thread, install on the worker, always clean up static Runnable withContext(Runnable task) { String captured = REQUEST_ID.get(); return () -> { String previous = REQUEST_ID.get(); REQUEST_ID.set(captured); try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous == null) REQUEST_ID.remove(); else REQUEST_ID.set(previous); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { REQUEST_ID.set("req-42"); pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("1. plain task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get())).get(); pool.submit(withContext(() -> System.out.println("2. wrapped task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get()))).get(); // a task that sets the ThreadLocal itself and forgets to remove it pool.submit(() -> REQUEST_ID.set("req-7")).get(); REQUEST_ID.remove(); // the next caller has no request pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("3. next task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get() + " (left over from an earlier task)")).get(); } } }

alt.title: ContextDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val requestId = ThreadLocal<String?>() // capture on the submitting thread, install on the worker, always clean up private fun withContext(task: () -> Unit): Runnable { val captured = requestId.get() return Runnable { val previous = requestId.get() requestId.set(captured) try { task() } finally { if (previous == null) requestId.remove() else requestId.set(previous) } } } /** A request id in a ThreadLocal, handed to a pool three ways. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> requestId.set("req-42") pool.submit { println("1. plain task sees: ${requestId.get()}") }.get() pool.submit(withContext { println("2. wrapped task sees: ${requestId.get()}") }).get() // a task that sets the ThreadLocal itself and forgets to remove it pool.submit { requestId.set("req-7") }.get() requestId.remove() // the next caller has no request pool.submit { println("3. next task sees: ${requestId.get()} (left over from an earlier task)") }.get() } }

try.expect: Line 1 prints null: the plain task runs on a pool thread that never saw req-42. Line 2 prints req-42, because the wrapper captured it on main. Line 3 prints req-7, left over from the earlier task that set the ThreadLocal and never removed it. The new caller had no request at all.

sections.h: Watch the queue, the active count, rejections and time in queue
sections.html:
A pool is a queue in front of a few threads, and it is the first place a slow dependency shows up. Four numbers tell you most of what you need.

The queue size, getQueue().size(). A queue that keeps growing means tasks arrive faster than they finish. Little's law from lesson 3 of this track says the wait grows with it.

The active count, getActiveCount(), compared with the maximum. A pool pinned at its maximum for minutes is saturated, and it's usually waiting on something downstream rather than working.

Rejections. ThreadPoolExecutor doesn't count them for you. Wrap the RejectedExecutionHandler in one that increments a counter and then throws, as MetricsDemo does. Every rejection is a request you turned away, so alert on it.

Time in queue. This is latency the caller feels and the task never measures. Record the time when a task is submitted, in the same wrapper that carries the context, and compare it when the task starts.

The getters are approximate. The Javadoc says so, because the threads keep changing them while you read. That's fine for a dashboard and wrong for program logic. Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics binds most of these numbers for you.

Of the four, queue time and rejections are what your customers feel. A pool with an empty queue and no rejections is healthy, however busy its threads look.

try.title: Read a pool's dashboard
steps: MetricsDemo sends 10 tasks of 300 ms to a pool with 2 threads and a queue of 4. Predict how many are rejected, and when the queue empties.
Run it and read the table row by row.

code.title: MetricsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 10 tasks of 300 ms hit a pool of 2 threads with a queue of 4. Watch the numbers a dashboard would show. */ public class MetricsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { LongAdder rejected = new LongAdder(); ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4), Thread.ofPlatform().name("auth-", 0).factory(), (task, executor) -> { rejected.increment(); // count it, then fail like AbortPolicy throw new RejectedExecutionException("auth pool full"); }); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { try { pool.execute(() -> sleep(300)); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // the caller would answer 503 here } } System.out.println(" ms threads active queued done rejected"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { System.out.printf("%4d %7d %6d %6d %4d %8d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size(), pool.getCompletedTaskCount(), rejected.sum()); sleep(200); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.html: package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder /** 10 tasks of 300 ms hit a pool of 2 threads with a queue of 4. Watch the numbers a dashboard would show. */ fun main() { val rejected = LongAdder() val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(4), Thread.ofPlatform().name("auth-", 0).factory()) { _, _ -> rejected.increment() // count it, then fail like AbortPolicy throw RejectedExecutionException("auth pool full") } repeat(10) { try { pool.execute { Thread.sleep(300) } } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { // the caller would answer 503 here } } println(" ms threads active queued done rejected") val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(6) { println("%4d %7d %6d %6d %4d %8d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.poolSize, pool.activeCount, pool.queue.size, pool.completedTaskCount, rejected.sum())) Thread.sleep(200) } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) }

try.expect: Two tasks run, four wait in the queue and four are rejected right away (2 + 4 = 6 accepted). Every 300 ms two more finish: the queue goes 4, 2, 0 while done climbs 0, 2, 4, 6, and active drops to 0 after about 900 ms. The rejected count stays at 4.

sections.h: Pool-induced deadlock: tasks that wait for tasks in the same pool
sections.html:
Here is a statement job that works in every test:

Java
pool.submit(() -> {
    Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> ledger.lines(merchant));   // a task inside a task
    return render(merchant, lines.get());                                     // waits for it
});
Kotlin
pool.submit<String> {
    val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { ledger.lines(merchant) }   // a task inside a task
    render(merchant, lines.get())                                     // waits for it
}

With 20 threads and 5 merchants, it's fine. At month-end it gets 400 merchants. The first 20 statement tasks take all 20 threads. Each one submits its fetch, and the fetches join the back of the queue, behind 380 statement tasks. Every thread now waits for a task that can only run on a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. The CPU drops to zero. Nothing throws. A thread dump shows no "deadlock found" line, because no lock is involved: every thread is just WAITING in FutureTask.get. Java Concurrency in Practice calls this thread starvation deadlock.

Three fixes, in the order I'd try them:

  1. Don't block inside the pool. Compose: supplyAsync(() -> ledger.lines(m), pool).thenApply(lines -> render(m, lines)). The render step runs as a callback when the fetch completes, so no thread waits. Only the caller joins at the end.
  2. Don't split what doesn't need splitting. If the statement task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline in the same task.
  3. Give each stage its own pool. Statement tasks may wait for a separate fetch pool, as long as fetch tasks never wait for the statement pool. That's a bulkhead from lesson 3.

A cached pool with no thread limit also makes the hang go away, by starting a thread for every waiting task. That moves the problem to memory and to the database connection pool. join() inside a CompletableFuture stage is the same bug, which is why lesson 6 of this track warned against it.

try.title: Hang a pool on purpose
steps: Run DeadlockDemo: two statement tasks on a pool of two threads, each waiting for a fast fetch on the same pool. Read the active and queued counts.
Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which composes the fetch and the render with CompletableFuture. Predict how long it takes.

code.title: DeadlockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** Two statement tasks on a 2-thread pool, each waiting for a fetch on the same pool. Pass "fixed" to compose instead. */ public class DeadlockDemo { static List<String> fetchLines(String merchant) { return List.of(merchant + "-1", merchant + "-2"); // fast: the problem isn't speed } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("stmt-", 0).factory()); try { if (fixed) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> statements = List.of("m1", "m2").stream() .map(m -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchLines(m), pool) .thenApply(lines -> m + ": " + lines.size() + " lines")) // nobody waits inside the pool .toList(); statements.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s.join())); return; } List<Future<String>> statements = List.of("m1", "m2").stream() .map(m -> pool.submit(() -> { Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> fetchLines(m)); // queued behind us return m + ": " + lines.get().size() + " lines"; // waits for it })) .toList(); Thread.sleep(300); ThreadPoolExecutor tpe = (ThreadPoolExecutor) pool; System.out.printf("after 300 ms: active=%d, queued=%d, completed=%d%n", tpe.getActiveCount(), tpe.getQueue().size(), tpe.getCompletedTaskCount()); try { System.out.println(statements.get(0).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { System.out.println("no statement after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start"); } } finally { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the stuck get() calls } } }

Pass "fixed" to compose instead. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("stmt-", 0).factory()) try { if (fixed) { val statements = listOf("m1", "m2").map { m -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fetchLines(m) }, pool) .thenApply { lines -> "$m: ${lines.size} lines" } // nobody waits inside the pool } statements.forEach { println(it.join()) } return } val statements = listOf("m1", "m2").map { m -> pool.submit<String> { val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { fetchLines(m) } // queued behind us "$m: ${lines.get().size} lines" // waits for it } } Thread.sleep(300) val tpe = pool as ThreadPoolExecutor println("after 300 ms: active=${tpe.activeCount}, queued=${tpe.queue.size}, completed=${tpe.completedTaskCount}") try { println(statements[0].get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { println("no statement after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start") } } finally { pool.shutdownNow() // interrupts the stuck get() calls } }

sections.h: Shut down in order, with a deadline
sections.html:
When Kubernetes stops a pod it sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 seconds unless you change it) and then kills the process. Everything in flight has to finish, or be recorded as lost, inside that window. The order matters:

Java
void stop() throws InterruptedException {
    intake.stop();                                                      // 1. no new work comes in
    long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(20);   //    inside the 30 s grace period
    for (ExecutorService pool : List.of(authPool, ledgerPool)) {        // 2. upstream first: auth feeds ledger
        pool.shutdown();
        long left = Math.max(0, deadline - System.nanoTime());
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(left, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
            List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow();           // 3. interrupt what is still running
            log.warn("{} tasks never started", neverStarted.size());    // 4. say what was lost
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
fun stop() {
    intake.stop()                                                       // 1. no new work comes in
    val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(20)     //    inside the 30 s grace period
    for (pool in listOf(authPool, ledgerPool)) {                        // 2. upstream first: auth feeds ledger
        pool.shutdown()
        val left = maxOf(0L, deadline - System.nanoTime())
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(left, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
            val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow()                       // 3. interrupt what is still running
            log.warn("{} tasks never started", neverStarted.size)       // 4. say what was lost
        }
    }
}

Stop intake first: pause the Kafka consumer, or fail the readiness probe so the load balancer stops sending requests. Otherwise new work keeps arriving at pools that are trying to drain.

Then shut pools down upstream first. authPool's tasks submit into ledgerPool. Shut down ledgerPool first and the authorizations still running in authPool get a RejectedExecutionException when they try to post to the ledger, which turns a clean shutdown into half-finished payments.

Give the whole sequence one deadline, shorter than the grace period, and share it between the pools. When a pool misses it, shutdownNow() interrupts what is still running and returns the tasks that never started. Log them, with request ids if your wrapper keeps them, so somebody can replay them. Don't forget the schedulers from lesson 5: after shutdown() their periodic tasks stop, which is what you want.

In Quarkus, put this in a method that observes ShutdownEvent, or in a @PreDestroy method on the bean that owns the pools. Never leave a pool for garbage collection to clean up: its threads keep it alive.

analogy: Running pools in production is like running a busy restaurant kitchen. Name tags on every cook (thread names) let you see who is stuck. An order ticket travels with each dish (the request context), and every cook throws the old ticket away before taking the next one. The board by the pass shows how many tickets are waiting (queue size) and how many customers were turned away (rejections). The deadlock is two cooks who each started a dish that needs a sauce, put the sauce order at the back of the queue, and stand waiting for it, while nobody is left to make sauce. The analogy breaks at closing time: a kitchen can tell customers to leave. A pool has to stop its own intake first, then let each station finish in order, and it gets one fixed deadline from the orchestrator.
world: In a payment service, a named pool per dependency (issuer-, ledger-, fraud-) turns a thread dump during an incident into a map: 40 issuer- threads in a socket read means the issuer is slow, not your code. Put the request id or idempotency key in the MDC at the edge, and make every pool carry it, so a ledger write logged on ledger-7 can be traced back to the authorization that caused it. Count rejections on the authorization pool and alert on them, because each one is a declined payment. Settlement and statement jobs are where pool-induced deadlock likes to live: nested fan-outs on one shared pool that only hang at month-end volume. On shutdown, pause the Kafka consumer before draining the pools, so no offset is committed for work that never ran, and remember that a Temporal worker factory needs its own shutdown call, so activities in flight can finish.
mistake: The most common mistake is fire-and-forget with submit: pool.submit(() -> audit.write(event)) with nobody keeping the Future. The audit write starts failing on a schema change, every exception sits in a Future that is garbage the moment it's created, and nothing is logged for days. People use submit because it's the method they know, and the failure path never runs in tests. Use execute for fire-and-forget work, or better, run every pool through a wrapper that reports failures from both execute and submit with the request id, the way the lab's ProductionPool does.

java.html: static Executor withMdc(Executor delegate) { return task -> { Map<String, String> captured = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); // 1. on the submitting thread delegate.execute(() -> { Map<String, String> previous = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); if (captured != null) MDC.setContextMap(captured); else MDC.clear(); // 2. on the worker try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous != null) MDC.setContextMap(previous); else MDC.clear(); // 3. never leak } }); }; } CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> ledger.post(entry), withMdc(ledgerPool));

kotlin.title: MdcCoroutine.kt (kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j)
kotlin.html: // MDCContext() copies the MDC now and installs it every time the coroutine // runs, on whichever thread that is, then restores the thread's own MDC scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO + MDCContext()) { ledger.post(entry) delay(100) // may resume on another thread log.info("posted") // the request id is still in the MDC } // the same idea for your own ThreadLocal scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO + requestId.asContextElement(value = "req-42")) { /* ... */ }

compare.note: The Java wrapper installs the context once, because a task stays on one thread from start to finish. A coroutine can move to another thread at every suspension point, so a wrapper around the whole coroutine wouldn't be enough. MDCContext() and asContextElement are thread context elements: the dispatcher installs the value each time the coroutine resumes on a thread and restores the thread's old value when it suspends. One trap: an MDC.put inside the coroutine is lost at the next suspension, because the element keeps reinstalling the map it captured. The kotlinx docs say to wrap the change in withContext(MDCContext()).

worked.title: Diagnose a statement job that stopped at month-end

steps.say: The month-end statement job has produced nothing for 30 minutes. CPU on the pod is near zero. A thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) shows all 20 stmt- threads in the same place. Before reading on, say what they are waiting for.
steps.code:
"stmt-3" #41 prio=5 os_prio=0 ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
	- parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)
	at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(...)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.awaitDone(...)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(...)
	at com.acme.settlement.StatementJob.lambda$run$0(StatementJob.java)
	...

steps.say: Every thread is inside a statement task, parked in FutureTask.get(), waiting for another task's result. The pool's metrics finish the story: active=20, the queue at 380 and not moving, completed flat. The awaited fetch tasks are in that queue, behind the other statement tasks, and they need a free thread that will never come. The dump has no "Found one Java-level deadlock" line, because the detector looks for cycles of locks, and a Future has no owner.
The fix is to stop holding a thread while waiting. Compose the fetch and the render, start every merchant's pipeline, and let only the job's own thread wait at the end.
steps.code: List<CompletableFuture<String>> statements = merchants.stream() .map(m -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> ledger.lines(m), pool) // 1. fetch on the pool .thenApply(lines -> render(m, lines))) // 2. render as a callback .toList(); return statements.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList(); // 3. only the caller waits

alt.html: val statements = merchants.map { m -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ ledger.lines(m) }, pool) // 1. fetch on the pool .thenApply { lines -> render(m, lines) } // 2. render as a callback } return statements.map { it.join() } // 3. only the caller waits

steps.say: Then make the next incident shorter. The stmt- names already paid off: they showed at once which pool was stuck. Add a dashboard panel and an alert for the queue size and the oldest task's wait on this pool, so a queue that stops moving pages someone within minutes, not after the merchants complain.

lab.title: A production pool, and a deadlock to fix
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The two StatementJob tests time out after 5 seconds: that is the deadlock.
Write ProductionPool.create: build the factory with Thread.ofPlatform().name(name + "-", 0).factory() and pass it to the private constructor, which already sets up the bounded queue.

Write ProductionPool.execute. Read RequestContext.get() first, on the calling thread. Then call super.execute with a lambda that saves the worker's own context, sets the captured id, runs the task, and restores the saved context in a finally.

Report failures inside that lambda: catch RuntimeException | Error from task.run() and report it without rethrowing. After run() returns, if the task is a Future whose state() is FAILED, report exceptionNow().
Fix StatementJob.run: start a supplyAsync(fetch, pool).thenApply(render) pipeline for every merchant, then join them all on the calling thread.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: Capture the id before super.execute. Inside the lambda you are already on the worker, where RequestContext.get() returns the worker's value.
task instanceof Future<?> f && f.state() == Future.State.FAILED (JDK 19+), then f.exceptionNow(), gives you the original exception, not an ExecutionException.
If reportsExecuteFailures sees the next task on ledger-1, your wrapper rethrew: the worker died and the pool replaced it.
The StatementJob fix needs no second pool. A thenApply callback never holds a thread while it waits.

drill.title: A context-carrying executor from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Executor withRequestId(Executor delegate): every task runs with the RequestContext of the thread that called execute, and the worker's own value is restored afterwards. Then compare. Where did you read the context, and is the restore in a finally?

answer.title: Contexts.java
answer.html: static Executor withRequestId(Executor delegate) { return task -> { String captured = RequestContext.get(); // on the caller's thread delegate.execute(() -> { String previous = RequestContext.get(); RequestContext.set(captured); // on the worker try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear(); else RequestContext.set(previous); } }); }; }

alt.title: Contexts.kt
alt.html: fun withRequestId(delegate: Executor) = Executor { task -> val captured = RequestContext.get() // on the caller's thread delegate.execute { val previous = RequestContext.get() RequestContext.set(captured) // on the worker try { task.run() } finally { if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear() else RequestContext.set(previous) } } }

recap: Name every pool's threads (Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory() on JDK 21+), so dumps and logs say which pool is stuck.
An UncaughtExceptionHandler only sees execute failures; submit hides them in the Future. Wrap execute once to report both, with the request id.
ThreadLocal context (MDC, tracing, security) doesn't follow a task to a pool. Capture it at submission, install it in the worker, restore it in finally.
Watch queue size, active count against the maximum, rejections and time in queue. Count rejections yourself in the handler.
A task that blocks on another task in the same bounded pool can hang the pool forever. Compose instead, do the work inline, or give each stage its own pool.
Shut down in order: stop intake, then pools upstream first, all within one deadline inside the grace period; log what shutdownNow returns.

explain.prompt: A teammate's statement job works with 5 merchants and hangs with 400, on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Explain what is happening and two ways to fix it.
explain.answer: Each merchant task submits its ledger fetch to the same pool and blocks on get(). With 400 merchants, the first 20 tasks take every thread, and their fetches are queued behind the other 380 merchant tasks. A fetch can only run on a free thread, and every thread is waiting for a fetch, so nothing ever finishes. The CPU is idle and nothing throws, because no lock is involved. One fix is to stop blocking inside the pool: start supplyAsync(fetch, pool).thenApply(render) for each merchant, so rendering is a callback and only the job's own thread waits at the end. Another is to run the fetches on a separate pool, so the statement threads wait on a pool that never waits back on them. Simplest of all, if the statement task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline.

deeper.html:
Why is the JVM's deadlock detector silent? jcmd <pid> Thread.print (and ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads) look for cycles of threads that each hold a lock another one needs: monitors from synchronized, and ownable synchronizers such as ReentrantLock. A thread waiting in Future.get() parks on the future, which has no owner, so there is no cycle to find. Names and stack traces are your only tools, which is one more reason to name threads.

The ThreadPoolExecutor Javadoc shows a second way to catch failures: override the afterExecute hook, which runs on the worker after each task:

Java
@Override
protected void afterExecute(Runnable r, Throwable t) {
    super.afterExecute(r, t);
    if (t == null && r instanceof Future<?> f && f.isDone()) {
        try {
            f.get();
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            t = e;
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            t = e.getCause();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
    if (t != null) log.error("task failed on {}", Thread.currentThread().getName(), t);
}
Kotlin
override fun afterExecute(r: Runnable, t: Throwable?) {
    super.afterExecute(r, t)
    var failure = t
    if (failure == null && r is Future<*> && r.isDone) {
        try {
            r.get()
        } catch (e: CancellationException) {
            failure = e
        } catch (e: ExecutionException) {
            failure = e.cause
        } catch (e: InterruptedException) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt()
        }
    }
    if (failure != null) log.error("task failed on {}", Thread.currentThread().name, failure)
}

It works, with two limits. It can't stop an execute failure from killing the worker, because the exception is rethrown after the hook runs. And it doesn't know the submitter's request id unless a wrapper stored it. That's why the lab wraps execute. Its sister hook, beforeExecute(Thread, Runnable), is the natural place to measure time in queue, and terminated() runs once when the pool has fully stopped.
